newsitem.title: KENYA: Population growth seen damaging Kenya smallholders.
newsitem.headline: Population growth seen damaging Kenya smallholders.

text.p: Population growth threatens the presence of smallholders in Kenya's coffee industry, an estates manager said on Tuesday.
Standard Chartered Estates Management said in a report that population growth, currently estimated at 3.4 percent, continued to reduce the land available for cash crops such as coffee.
"In the long-run, the units of land where coffee is grown will become too small and subsistence farming will be given priority in most households," the report said.
"Thus production from the smallholder will steadily decline as the country endeavours to keep up with population growth."
Kenya's planning and national development ministry estimated Kenya's 1996 population at 28.3 million. Most of these people live in the fertile highlands where coffee and tea are grown.
Some 300,000 smallholders produce an estimated 65 percent of Kenya's coffee and are responsible for its high quality, the Coffee Board of Kenya says. Estates produce just 35 percent.
Standard Chartered Estates Management said proposals for improvement of the smallholder sector should be seen as a temporary step towards improved coffee output.

The report pointed that in the years following the 1989 collapse of the International Coffee Agreement production among smallholders fell by 46 percent compared to 12 percent for estates. This indicated that smallholders were highly vulnerable to sharp changes in export prices.

"It is evident that the national economy could be adversely affected if the bulk of the country's coffee production remained in the smallholders sector. Reduced extension services to that sector makes the situation even worse," the report said.

"We believe that estates expansion in new coffee areas is a sure way of achieving increased and sustained productivity. The expansion of the estates sector in the new areas would take advantage of existing technology, such as irrigation, mechanised machinery and high input use," the report added.
Smallholder farms average 0.4 hectares whereas estates range anywhere between four and 200 hectares.

"Low input use within the smallholder sub-sector leads to crop losses mainly through nutritional stress and disease. This problem is compounded by the lack of adequate and effective credit facilities for seasonal crop finance," it said.
